abstract: |
  The Eastern Oyster (Crassostrea virginica) has been well studied for it's ecological significance within coastal estuarine systems. As such, much effort has been put into restoring oyster habitat throughout the Atlantic and Gulf of America (Mexico) coastal regions. In an attempt to achieve maximum success, many researchers and stakeholders have turned to habitat suitability models (HSMs) to help delineate the most favorable areas for oyster habitat success. One such HSM often employed is the Habitat Suitability Index (HSI), which often rely on user input to determine model variables and their associated importance. To avoid any potentially un-intended subjectivity or bias, this paper aims to evaluate of utilizing an alternative method known as Maximum Entropy (MaxEnt). MaxEnt is often used in species distribution modeling (SDM) to take known conditions at known species occurrence locations to determine the habitat suitability of a region by using empirical and statistical relationships. This paper aims to explore the feasibility of using a SDM to map habitat suitability in the Pensacola Bay System (Pensacola, FL), and compare it to an existing HSI from the same area to determine if the model can serve as a supplemental dataset or even as a replacement to currently employed methods.
